title: Language core: OOP, equality and hashing (Java)
seriesDescription: Interfaces, abstract classes, records and sealed types, composition over inheritance, equals and hashCode. JEE-Advanced style: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code and multi-correct questions.
description: Interfaces vs abstract classes, records, sealed types, default-method diamonds, composition over inheritance, overloading vs overriding and the equals/hashCode contract with its mutable-key traps.
source: Oracle Java Tutorials; JLS 8.4.8, 9.4.1.3, 15.12; Effective Java (Bloch) items 10, 11, 18; Baeldung; Toptal and GeeksforGeeks Java interview lists

questions.prompt: In Java, which of these can declare ordinary mutable instance fields (per-object state) that its subclasses inherit?

options.why: Interface fields are implicitly public static final constants, so there is no per-object mutable state.
A record can only have the components in its header as instance fields, and they are final; it cannot be extended anyway.
Correct: an abstract class is a normal class that cannot be instantiated, so it may hold state, constructors and concrete methods.
Sealing restricts who may implement it, but it is still an interface with no instance fields.

questions.explanation: Interface vs abstract class is the classic opener. Interfaces (even with default methods, Java 8+) have no instance state and a class may implement many; an abstract class carries state and constructor logic but a class can extend only one.

questions.prompt: Match each Java construct to what it is for.

right.text: Compact immutable data carrier with generated `equals`, `hashCode` and `toString`
Closed hierarchy: only the classes named in `permits` may extend it
Gives implementing classes a ready-made method body without a shared superclass
Cannot be instantiated but may hold per-object state and constructors for subclasses
A fixed set of named instances that no other code can extend
Automatically makes every field lazily loaded

questions.explanation: Records, sealed types and enums model closed or value-like data; default methods evolve interfaces; abstract classes share state.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the option that fits.
questions.assertion: Inheritance couples a subclass to its superclass more tightly than composition couples a wrapper to a collaborator.
questions.reason: A subclass can depend on implementation details of the superclass, such as which overridable methods call each other.

whys.a: Correct: the fragile base class problem is exactly this hidden dependence, which a wrapper that only uses the public API avoids.
whys.b: R is not merely true, it is the reason A holds.
whys.c: R is true: self-use of overridable methods is a documented source of bugs.
whys.d: A is true; Effective Java item 18 says to favour composition over inheritance.

questions.explanation: Effective Java: design for inheritance or prohibit it. Composition plus delegation (forwarding class) keeps the dependency to the public contract.

questions.prompt: A subclass of `HashSet<String>` counts additions: `add(e)` does `count++` then `super.add(e);` `addAll(c)` does `count += c.size()` then `super.addAll(c)`. After one call `addAll(List.of("a","b","c"))` on a new instance, what is `count`?
questions.explanation: `HashSet.addAll` (inherited from `AbstractCollection`) calls the overridden `add` for every element, so each element is counted twice: 3 + 3 = 6. This is the textbook case for composition over inheritance. (Verified by running it.)

questions.prompt: Complete the sentence about the equals and hashCode contract.
questions.text: The equals contract requires it to be reflexive, {1}, transitive and consistent; if a.equals(b) is true then a.hashCode() must be {2} to b.hashCode(); a record generates both methods from its {3}.
questions.explanation: Equal objects must have equal hashes; unequal objects may share a hash. Records derive `equals/hashCode` from their components.

questions.prompt:
```java
Integer a = 127, b = 127, c = 128, d = 128;
```

How many of the four expressions `a == b`, `c == d`, `c.equals(d)`, `a.equals(b)` evaluate to true?
questions.explanation: Autoboxing uses `Integer.valueOf`, which caches `-128..127`, so `a == b` is true but `c == d` compares two distinct objects and is false. Both `equals` calls are true: 3 true. (Verified by running it.)

checks.label: checks the type with instanceof or getClass

questions.explanation: A `record Point(int x, int y)` generates all of this. `getClass()` versus `instanceof` is a debate: `instanceof` is fine for a final class. Other correct spellings (`31 * x + y`) also pass.

questions.prompt: Write a Java record named `Pair` with a String component name and an int component age.
questions.explanation: A record header declares the components; the compiler adds private final fields, accessors, equals, hashCode and toString.

options.why: The entry was filed under the hash of `[1]`; after the mutation the hash is different, so the lookup goes to another bucket.
Correct: the entry is still in the map (size 1) but is unreachable by either the mutated key or an equal new list.
`containsKey` would only be true if the entry were found; it sits in the bucket of the old hash.
Mutating a key never removes the entry, and `get(k)` cannot succeed here.

questions.explanation: Never use a mutable object as a `HashMap` key (or `HashSet` element) if its `hashCode` depends on mutable state. The entry becomes a leak: present but unfindable. (Verified by running it.)

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the option that fits.
questions.assertion: If a class overrides `equals()` but not `hashCode()`, two equal objects can both end up in the same `HashSet`.
questions.reason: The `hashCode()` contract requires a different hash value for every pair of unequal objects.

whys.a: R is false, so it cannot explain A.
whys.b: R is false: the contract only demands equal objects have equal hashes.
whys.c: Correct: A is true because the default identity hashCode usually sends equal objects to different buckets; R is false (collisions between unequal objects are allowed).
whys.d: A is true, so this option is wrong.

questions.explanation: Contract: equal objects must have equal hash codes; unequal objects may share a hash code (it only affects performance).

questions.prompt: Select all that are safe to use as `HashMap` keys (value-based equality, hash stable over time).

options.why: Immutable, value-based equals, and the hash is cached.
Records get value-based `equals/hashCode` from immutable components.
Immutable with value-based equality.
Its hashCode changes with its contents, so the entry gets lost.
It does not override `equals/hashCode`, so lookups only work by identity, and its contents are mutable.

questions.explanation: Immutable value types make good keys. Identity-hashed mutable objects only match themselves, and content-hashed mutable ones break when they change.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the option that fits.
questions.assertion: A Java record is implicitly final.
questions.reason: The `equals` method of a record compares all of its components.

whys.a: Both are true, but the equality semantics have nothing to do with why records cannot be extended.
whys.b: Correct: records are final (they cannot be subclassed), and generated equals compares components, but one does not explain the other.
whys.d: A is true: record classes are implicitly final.

questions.explanation: Records are shallowly immutable data carriers: final class, final fields, accessors, and component-based `equals`/hashCode/toString.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the option that fits.
questions.assertion: A Java class can extend several abstract classes at the same time.
questions.reason: A Java class can implement several interfaces at the same time.

whys.a: This option says both statements are true and R explains A, which does not match: A is false because Java has single inheritance of classes; R is true, and it is the reason interfaces are used for multiple types.
whys.b: This option says both statements are true but R does not explain A, which does not match: A is false because Java has single inheritance of classes; R is true, and it is the reason interfaces are used for multiple types.
whys.c: This option says A is true and R is false, which does not match: A is false because Java has single inheritance of classes; R is true, and it is the reason interfaces are used for multiple types.
whys.d: Correct: A is false because Java has single inheritance of classes; R is true, and it is the reason interfaces are used for multiple types.

questions.explanation: Single class inheritance avoids state diamonds; multiple interface inheritance is allowed because interfaces carry no instance state.

options.text: Compile error: `D` inherits unrelated defaults for `who()` and must override it
options.why: Correct: `B` and `C` each override `A.who()`, so neither is more specific and the class must resolve the conflict.

options.text: It compiles and `who()` returns `"B"`, because `B` is listed first
options.why: Declaration order never resolves a default-method conflict.

options.text: It compiles and `who()` returns `"A"`, the common ancestor
options.why: A is overridden by both `B` and `C`, so it is not the winner.

options.text: It compiles and throws an error at run time on the first call
options.why: The conflict is detected at compile time, not at run time.

questions.explanation: Fix it by overriding: `public String who() { return B.super.who(); }`. Rule: a class wins over interfaces, a more specific interface wins over a less specific one, otherwise you must override.

questions.prompt: A Java class can implement several interfaces but can extend only one class.

options.why: Correct: Java has single class inheritance and multiple interface inheritance.
The rule is exactly this; multiple class inheritance is what is forbidden.

questions.explanation: Single inheritance of state avoids ambiguous fields; interfaces carry no instance state.

questions.prompt: A field declared in a Java interface is an ordinary per-object field that each implementing instance can change.

options.why: Interface fields are implicitly public static final constants, not per-object state.
Correct: interface fields are constants shared by all implementers.

questions.explanation: Per-object mutable state needs an abstract or concrete class.

options.text: `OSS, since only f(x) is bound to the Object overload`
options.why: Correct: overloads are chosen at compile time from the static type, so `f(x)` is O; `"hi"` and `null` both pick the most specific `f(String)`.

options.text: `SSS, since the runtime type of x decides the overload`
options.why: Wrong: x has static type `Object`, so the compiler binds `f(x)` to `f(Object)` even though the runtime object is a `String`.

options.text: `OOS, since a string literal prefers the Object overload`
options.why: Wrong: a string literal has static type `String`, so f(`"hi"`) binds to the more specific overload and prints S.

options.text: `Compile error, since the call f(null) is ambiguous`
options.why: Wrong: `String` is more specific than `Object`, so `f(null)` is not ambiguous; it would be ambiguous only for unrelated types like `String` and `Integer`.

questions.explanation: Overloads resolve at compile time on the static type; overrides resolve at run time on the actual class. This is the standard "overloading vs overriding" interview trap.

options.why: Correct: field access uses the static type (`P.n` is "P") while the overridden method is dispatched on the real class (`C.get()` is "C").
Wrong: fields are not polymorphic; a subclass field with the same name hides the parent field rather than overriding it.
Wrong: `get()` is an instance method and is overridden, so the call runs `C.get()` even though the reference type is P.
Wrong: this swaps the two rules; the field follows the reference type and the method follows the object type.

questions.explanation: Only instance methods are dispatched dynamically. Fields, static methods and private methods are bound by the static type, so avoid redeclaring fields in subclasses.
